    In the year 1500, the world was a vastly different place. The Black Death had ravaged Europe, leaving behind a power vacuum that was filled by the remnants of the feudal system. The nobility, who had once been the ruling class, had been reduced to vassals, forced to swear fealty to the strongest lords.


    The great lords, in turn, had become the de facto rulers of the land. They wielded absolute power, collecting taxes, maintaining armies, and dispensing justice. The peasants, who had once been the backbone of the economy, were now forced to work long hours in the fields, toiling for their lords' benefit.


    The cities, once hubs of commerce and innovation, had been reduced to mere backwaters. The merchants, who had once been the driving force behind trade and progress, were now forced to operate under the strictures of the feudal system. They were subject to the whims of the lords, who controlled the flow of goods and information.


    The arts and sciences had also suffered. The great universities, which had once been centers of learning and discovery, had been shut down or forced to operate in secret. The nobility, who had once been patrons of the arts, had become increasingly repressive, suppressing any dissent or criticism.

    In the cities, the merchants were beginning to chafe against their restrictive roles. They were forming guilds, seeking to improve their lot and gain more power. They were also beginning to trade with other cities, seeking to expand their influence and challenge the lords' control.
